Name: Bug / Unexpected Behavior
Keywords: bug, error, exception, crash, broken, wrong output, fails, failing, not working, stack trace, traceback, regression, unexpected, null pointer, undefined, cannot read, type error, blank page, white screen, 500 error, panic, fix, lỗi, sửa lỗi, bị lỗi, không chạy, sai kết quả
Description: Something produces the wrong result, errors or crashes, and the cause is not yet known.
Define: Write expected vs actual behavior and the exact repro: command, input, environment. Gate: a failing automated test or a one-command repro that you ran and saw fail.
Decompose: Trace the path from input to wrong output through each layer. Find where the data first goes wrong. List what changed recently (commits, deploys, dependency bumps, config).
Prioritize: Rank hypotheses by likelihood and cost to test; test cheap, likely ones first. Recent changes and the first point where data is wrong come first.
Plan: For each hypothesis write the observation that would confirm or kill it. If it is a regression, pick a known-good and known-bad commit for bisect.
Execute: Test one hypothesis at a time and log the result. Narrow with bisect or divide-and-conquer until one change explains the bug. Fix the root cause, not the symptom.
Verify: The Step 1 repro or test now passes; full suite, lint and type checks pass. Search the codebase for the same faulty pattern.
Communicate: PR: root cause in one sentence, the fix, why it is safe, and the regression test that now guards it.
Techniques: Read the Error Carefully; Minimal Reproduction; Check Recent Changes; Git Bisect; Divide and Conquer; Hypothesis Log; Logging and Tracing; Differential Diagnosis
Biases: Anchoring on the First Clue; Confirmation Bias in Debugging; Streetlight Effect; Works on My Machine
Review Focus: Correctness; Edge Cases; Error Handling; Tests
Anti-Patterns: Changing code until the symptom disappears; catching and swallowing the exception; fixing without a test that failed first; several speculative changes at once.
Escalate: Users are affected in production right now: treat it as an incident and mitigate first. Expected behavior is unclear: confirm it with the user before fixing.

Name: New Feature
Keywords: add, implement, build, create, new feature, support, endpoint, page, screen, integrate, integration, user story, requirement, enable, thêm tính năng, xây dựng, làm chức năng, thêm chức năng
Description: Add behavior that does not exist yet.
Define: Restate the feature as user-visible behavior with 3-7 acceptance criteria (Given/When/Then), including error and empty cases, and list what is out of scope. Gate: criteria written and confirmed, or assumptions stated explicitly.
Decompose: Map which layers change (UI, API, domain, data, config), new versus modified interfaces, schema changes and new dependencies.
Prioritize: Pick a thin vertical slice that satisfies one criterion end to end; move nice-to-haves out; spike the riskiest unknown first.
Plan: Order the tasks with a test for each slice; decide feature flag, migration and rollback; note docs and config to update.
Execute: Per slice: failing acceptance or unit test, minimal code to pass, then refactor. Commit per slice and keep the build green.
Verify: Every acceptance criterion has a passing test; full suite, lint, type checks and build pass; try error and empty paths by hand.
Communicate: PR: what users can now do, how to try it, screenshots or examples, flags and follow-ups.
Techniques: Thin Vertical Slice; Spike; Feature Flag; Preparatory Refactoring
Testing: Acceptance Tests (Given/When/Then); TDD Red-Green-Refactor; Contract Tests
Principles: YAGNI; KISS; Separation of Concerns; Make Illegal States Unrepresentable
Biases: Planning Fallacy; Gold Plating; Golden Hammer
Review Focus: Correctness; Edge Cases; Security; API Compatibility; Tests; Readability
Anti-Patterns: One big-bang PR; building for hypothetical future needs; only the happy path; no error or empty states.
Escalate: Several viable designs with real trade-offs: run make-decision (/decide) and record an ADR before building.

Name: Refactor / Restructure
Keywords: refactor, clean up, cleanup, restructure, rename, extract, simplify, technical debt, tech debt, legacy, decouple, split module, spaghetti, duplicate code, reorganize code, tái cấu trúc, dọn code, nợ kỹ thuật, code rối
Description: Change the structure of code without changing its behavior.
Define: State the goal as the change it enables or a property it improves (coupling, duplication, size), and that behavior must not change. Gate: tests cover the code being moved; add characterization tests where they do not.
Decompose: Map dependencies in and out of the target: callers, imports, shared state. Find seams where code can be cut apart.
Prioritize: Order steps so each is small and keeps tests green; start with what unlocks the most (Mikado). Stop when the goal is met.
Plan: List refactoring steps (rename, extract, move, inline), each committable on its own. Plan expand-contract for public APIs.
Execute: One mechanical step at a time, tests after each, commit. Prefer IDE or codemod refactorings. Never mix behavior changes in.
Verify: Tests unchanged and green; public API compatibility checked; the diff shows no behavior change; the target property improved.
Communicate: PR: 'no behavior change' up front, the change it enables, and how to review it (commit by commit).
Techniques: Preparatory Refactoring; Mikado Method; Seams; Parallel Change (Expand-Contract); Strangler Fig; Codemod / Automated Refactoring; Dead Code Removal
Principles: Single Responsibility; Separation of Concerns; Dependency Direction; DRY (Rule of Three); KISS
Biases: Rewrite Fallacy; Sunk Cost on an Approach; Golden Hammer
Anti-Patterns: Refactoring without tests; mixing refactors with bug fixes or features; big-bang rewrites; abstracting before the third duplication.
Escalate: Rewrite versus incremental change, or a large restructure: run make-decision (/decide) and record an ADR.

Name: Performance / Scalability
Keywords: slow, slower, latency, spike, spiked, degraded, slow query, query, performance, throughput, memory, memory leak, leak, cpu, timeout, p95, p99, optimize, optimise, scale, scaling, n+1, cache, load, bottleneck, chậm, tối ưu, tốn bộ nhớ, rò rỉ bộ nhớ, hiệu năng
Description: Make code faster, lighter or able to handle more load.
Define: Name the metric, workload and target (for example p95 under 200 ms at 100 rps; memory flat over one hour). Gate: a repeatable benchmark or load test with a recorded baseline.
Decompose: Break total time or memory into parts (request path, database, network, CPU, GC, allocations) using profiles and traces, not guesses.
Prioritize: Pareto: attack the largest measured contributor first; prefer algorithmic and I/O fixes over micro-optimizations.
Plan: One optimization per experiment, with the expected gain and how it is measured. Check correctness risks such as cache invalidation.
Execute: Change one thing, rerun the same benchmark, record the numbers, keep or revert.
Verify: The benchmark meets the target against the baseline under the same conditions; tests pass; cost did not just move elsewhere (memory for CPU).
Communicate: PR: before/after numbers, method, environment and trade-offs.
Techniques: Profiling; Logging and Tracing; Divide and Conquer; Differential Diagnosis
Testing: Benchmark / Load Test; Regression Test First
Biases: Premature Optimization; Streetlight Effect; Confirmation Bias in Debugging
Anti-Patterns: Optimizing without a profile; benchmarks on unrepresentative data; caching without an invalidation plan; micro-optimizing something that is not the bottleneck.
Escalate: The fix needs an architecture change (queue, sharding, new datastore): run make-decision (/decide) and record an ADR.

Name: Flaky Test / CI Failure
Keywords: flaky, flaky test, intermittent, sometimes fails, randomly fails, ci red, ci failing, pipeline, nondeterministic, race condition, passes locally, fails in ci, timeout in ci, test chập chờn, ci lỗi, lúc được lúc không
Description: A test or pipeline fails sometimes, or only in CI.
Define: Record the failure rate and the exact failing assertion or log from CI. Gate: reproduce the failure by running the test repeatedly (50-200 runs), shuffled or under stress.
Decompose: Classify the source of nondeterminism: test order or shared state, time and clocks, concurrency, network or external services, resource limits, randomness, environment differences.
Prioritize: Test the categories that fit the failure signature first: timeouts point to resources or network, wrong values to shared state or ordering.
Plan: Make the failure frequent (loop, race detector, shuffle, CPU limits) so each hypothesis gives a fast signal.
Execute: Fix the cause: isolate state, inject the clock, wait for conditions instead of sleeping, stub the network.
Verify: Run the test the same number of times that reproduced it, with zero failures; the full CI suite passes; no test was disabled.
Communicate: PR: root cause, how it was reproduced, run counts before and after.
Techniques: Stress and Repeat; Differential Diagnosis; Logging and Tracing; Hypothesis Log; Minimal Reproduction
Principles: Determinism (Inject Time and Randomness); Fail Fast
Biases: Works on My Machine; Confirmation Bias in Debugging; Anchoring on the First Clue
Anti-Patterns: Adding retries or longer sleeps; skipping or quarantining the test; calling it an infra flake without evidence.
Escalate: The failure is in CI infrastructure rather than code: report it with the evidence and a proposed fix.

Name: Production Incident
Keywords: outage, down, incident, production, prod, sev1, sev2, customers affected, users affected, 5xx, 500s, rollback, hotfix, on-call, pager, degraded, sự cố, sập, production lỗi, hệ thống chết
Description: Something is broken in production and users are affected now.
Define: Impact first: who and what is affected, since when, how badly. Gate: a mitigation decision (rollback, flag off, scale up) within minutes; root-causing comes after impact stops.
Decompose: Line up the timeline of changes (deploys, config, traffic, dependencies) against symptom onset; find affected components from dashboards, logs and traces.
Prioritize: Mitigate, then diagnose, then fix, then prevent. Choose the fastest reversible mitigation.
Plan: Assign roles (lead, communications) and an update cadence; list mitigation options with their risks.
Execute: Apply the mitigation and confirm recovery in metrics; then reproduce and fix the root cause with a regression test.
Verify: Metrics back to baseline; the fix deployed and verified; alerts would catch a recurrence.
Communicate: Status updates during the incident; a blameless postmortem afterwards with timeline, root cause and action items.
Techniques: Check Recent Changes; Logging and Tracing; Differential Diagnosis; Feature Flag; Hypothesis Log
Biases: Anchoring on the First Clue; Confirmation Bias in Debugging
Anti-Patterns: Root-causing while users are still affected; unrecorded changes in production; blaming people.
Escalate: A business-level crisis beyond the code: use problem-solving-pro (/solve) with --category "Crisis / Turnaround".

Name: Migration / Upgrade
Keywords: migrate, migration, upgrade, version bump, bump, framework upgrade, deprecate, deprecated, move to, port, porting, database migration, schema change, breaking change, replace library, nâng cấp, chuyển đổi, di chuyển, đổi thư viện
Description: Move code, data or dependencies from one system or version to another.
Define: Source and target versions or systems, why, constraints (downtime, data size) and done criteria. Gate: an inventory of everything affected (usages, data, configs) with counts.
Decompose: Group affected items by type and risk (API changes, data, config, build). Read the changelog and migration guide for breaking changes.
Prioritize: Low-risk, high-coverage steps first; isolate data migrations; make every step deployable on its own.
Plan: Expand-contract or strangler sequence with a rollback for each step, backups for data, and codemods for repetitive edits.
Execute: Step by step behind a compatibility layer or flag; full tests per step; migrate data in batches with checks.
Verify: Tests pass on the target; data counts or checksums match; no deprecated usage remains (search for it); performance is comparable.
Communicate: Migration plan or runbook; one PR per step; changelog of breaking changes.
Techniques: Parallel Change (Expand-Contract); Strangler Fig; Branch by Abstraction; Codemod / Automated Refactoring; Feature Flag
Biases: Planning Fallacy; Rewrite Fallacy; Sunk Cost on an Approach
Anti-Patterns: Big-bang cutover without rollback; jumping several major versions at once; irreversible data changes first.
Escalate: Choosing the target technology: run make-decision (/decide) first.

Name: Code Review
Keywords: review, code review, pr review, review my code, check my code, audit, feedback on code, look over, critique, đánh giá code, review giúp, xem code
Description: Assess a change someone else (or you) wrote for defects and risks.
Define: Understand intent from the PR description and linked issue: what should change and what must not. Gate: a one-sentence summary of what the change is meant to do.
Decompose: Split the diff by concern (logic, tests, config, refactor) and mark risky areas (concurrency, security, data, public APIs).
Prioritize: Correctness and security first, then design, then tests, then style. Label every finding blocking or optional.
Plan: For each risky area decide how to verify it: run the tests, trace a real caller, try edge inputs.
Execute: Trace real callers and inputs through the change; go through the review checklist; run the code or tests where you can.
Verify: Every blocking finding has a concrete failure scenario (input, then wrong result); drop speculative findings.
Communicate: Findings ranked by severity, each with file:line, the scenario and a suggested fix; blocking separated from optional.
Techniques: Trace the Data Flow; Differential Diagnosis; Rubber Duck Explanation
Principles: KISS; Single Responsibility; Fail Fast; Principle of Least Surprise
Biases: Bikeshedding; Anchoring on the First Clue; Confirmation Bias in Debugging
Review Focus: Correctness; Edge Cases; Error Handling; Security; Concurrency; Performance; Data Safety; API Compatibility; Tests; Readability; Observability
Anti-Patterns: Nitpicking style while missing logic bugs; vague comments without a scenario; approving without reading the tests.
Escalate: A design disagreement rather than a defect: run make-decision (/decide) on the options.
